title: Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three

stories.title: 🔥 Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three
summaryBullets: They walked around in the midst of the flames, singing hymns to God and blessing the Lord. (1:1).
Then Azariah stood still in the fire and prayed aloud: (1:2).
“Blessed are you, O Lord, God of our ancestors, and worthy of praise, and glorious is your name forever! (1:3).
For you are just in all you have done; all your works are true and your ways right, and all your judgments are true. (1:4).
You have executed true judgments in all you have brought upon us and upon Jerusalem, the holy city of our ancestors; by a true judgment you have brought all this upon us because of our sins. (1:5).
For we have sinned and broken your law in turning away from you; in all matters we have sinned grievously. (1:6).
We have not obeyed your commandments; we have not kept them or done what you have commanded us for our own good. (1:7).
So all that you have brought upon us and all that you have done to us, you have done by a true judgment. (1:8).
You have handed us over to our enemies, lawless and hateful rebels, and to an unjust king, the most wicked in all the world. (1:9).
And now we cannot open our mouths; we, your servants who worship you, bear shame and reproach. (1:10).
For your name’s sake do not give us up forever, and do not annul your covenant. (1:11).
Do not withdraw your mercy from us, for the sake of Abraham your beloved and for the sake of Isaac your servant and Israel your holy one, (1:12).
to whom you promised to multiply their descendants like the stars of heaven and like the sand on the shore of the sea. (1:13).
For we, O Lord, have become fewer than any other nation and are brought low this day in all the world because of our sins. (1:14).
In our day we have no ruler, or prophet, or leader, no burnt offering, or sacrifice, or oblation, or incense, no place to make an offering before you and to find mercy. (1:15).
Yet with a contrite heart and a humble spirit may we be accepted, (1:16).

as though it were with burnt offerings of rams and bulls or with tens of thousands of fat lambs; such may our sacrifice be in your sight today, and may we unreservedly follow you, for no shame will come to those who trust in you. (1:17).
And now with all our heart we follow you; we fear you and seek your presence. (1:18).
Do not put us to shame, but deal with us in your patience and in your abundant mercy. (1:19).
Deliver us in accordance with your marvelous works, and bring glory to your name, O Lord. (1:20).
Let all who do harm to your servants be put to shame; let them be disgraced and deprived of all power, and let their strength be broken. (1:21).
Let them know that you alone are the Lord God, glorious over the whole world.” (1:22).
Now the king’s servants who threw them in kept stoking the furnace with naphtha, pitch, tinder, and brushwood. (1:23).
And the flames poured out above the furnace forty-nine cubits (1:24).
and spread out and burned those Chaldeans who were caught near the furnace. (1:25).
But the angel of the Lord came down into the furnace to be with Azariah and his companions and drove the fiery flame out of the furnace (1:26).
and made the inside of the furnace as though a moist wind were whistling through it. The fire did not touch them at all and caused them no pain or distress. (1:27).
Then the three with one voice praised and glorified and blessed God in the furnace: (1:28).
“Blessed are you, O Lord, God of our ancestors, and to be praised and highly exalted forever; And blessed is your glorious, holy name, and to be highly praised and highly exalted forever. (1:29).
Blessed are you in the temple of your holy glory, and to be extolled and highly glorified forever. (1:30).
Blessed are you who look into the depths from your throne on the cherubim, and to be praised and highly exalted forever. (1:31).
Blessed are you on the throne of your kingdom, and to be extolled and highly exalted forever. (1:32).
Blessed are you in the firmament of heaven, and to be sung and glorified forever. (1:33).
“Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:34).
Bless the Lord, you heavens; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:35).
Bless the Lord, you angels of the Lord; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:36).
Bless the Lord, all you waters above the heavens; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:37).
Bless the Lord, all you powers of the Lord; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:38).
Bless the Lord, sun and moon; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:39).
Bless the Lord, stars of heaven; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:40).
“Bless the Lord, all rain and dew; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:41).
Bless the Lord, all you winds; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:42).
Bless the Lord, fire and heat; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:43).
Bless the Lord, winter cold and summer heat; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:44).
Bless the Lord, dews and falling snow; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:45).
Bless the Lord, nights and days; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:46).
Bless the Lord, light and darkness; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:47).
Bless the Lord, ice and cold; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:48).
Bless the Lord, frosts and snows; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:49).
Bless the Lord, lightnings and clouds; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:50).
“Let the earth bless the Lord; let it sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:51).
Bless the Lord, mountains and hills; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:52).
Bless the Lord, all that grows in the ground; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:53).
Bless the Lord, seas and rivers; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:54).
Bless the Lord, you springs; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:55).
Bless the Lord, you sea monsters and all that swim in the waters; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:56).
Bless the Lord, all birds of the air; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:57).
Bless the Lord, all wild animals and cattle; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:58).
“Bless the Lord, all people on earth; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:59).
Bless the Lord, O Israel; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:60).
Bless the Lord, you priests of the Lord; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:61).
Bless the Lord, you servants of the Lord; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:62).
Bless the Lord, spirits and souls of the righteous; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:63).
Bless the Lord, you who are holy and humble in heart; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. (1:64).

“Bless the Lord, Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael; sing praise to him and highly exalt him forever. For he has rescued us from Hades and saved us from the power of death and delivered us from the midst of the burning fiery furnace; from the midst of the fire he has delivered us. (1:65).
Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever. (1:66).
All who worship the Lord, bless the God of gods, sing praise to him and give thanks to him, for his mercy endures forever.” (1:67).
crossRefs: Daniel 3:19-25: The furnace heated seven times over and a fourth figure walking in the fire.
Psalm 51:16-17: A broken and contrite heart offered where sacrifice is not desired.
Genesis 22:17: The promise to multiply descendants like the stars and the sand of the shore.
Psalm 148:1-14: Creation from the heights to the sea creatures summoned to praise the Lord.
Psalm 136:1: Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good; his mercy endures forever.

translationNotes.note: Four fuels, each chosen to burn hotter than wood. Naphtha is a light petroleum that seeps to the surface in Mesopotamia and lights instantly; pitch is bitumen; the third is tow, the coarse fiber combed off flax, which flashes like paper; the fourth is cut vine twigs. This is a stoked industrial fire, not a campfire.

A cubit is a unit of length, the forearm from elbow to fingertip, roughly eighteen inches. Flames pouring out forty-nine cubits above the furnace describes a column of fire about seventy-three feet high, which is why it caught the men standing near it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֲנַנְיָה (Hananyah), עֲזַרְיָה (Azaryah), מִישָׁאֵל (Mishaʾel) - Greek: Ανανιας (Ananias), Αζαριας (Azarias), Μισαηλ (Misael)
translationNotes.note: These are their Hebrew birth names, meaning roughly 'the Lord has been gracious,' 'the Lord has helped,' and 'who is what God is.' The Babylonian court had renamed them Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego (Daniel 1:7). The hymn calls them by the Hebrew names.

The section that summons all creation opens in Greek with the imperative eulogeite, 'bless.' Its Latin form, Benedicite, became the standing title for that canticle, which is used as a fixed morning canticle in Christian daily prayer.

stories.keyTakeaway: Azariah stands in the fire and prays, confessing Israel's sin and asking that a contrite heart be accepted as sacrifice. The king's servants stoke the furnace until its flames kill the Chaldeans nearby, an angel drives the flame out, and the three call all creation to bless the Lord.

intro:
The Prayer of Azariah and the Song of the Three does not name its author. It is the Greek addition to Daniel 3, set at the point where the three men have been bound and thrown into the furnace, between verses 23 and 24 of the Aramaic text. In the Greek and in the Vulgate it is not a separate book at all: its sixty-seven verses are numbered as Daniel 3, verses 24 to 90, after which the Aramaic narrative resumes at verse 91 and the chapter closes at a hundred verses, which is how the Douay-Rheims and other Vulgate-based Bibles print it. Like Susanna and Bel and the Dragon it survives in two Greek forms, the Old Greek and Theodotion's; Theodotion's is the one the churches adopted, and Jerome's prologue to Daniel records that the churches of Christ read this prophet according to Theodotion and not according to the Septuagint translators.

The addition has three parts. Azariah prays from inside the fire, confessing the nation's sin and asking that a contrite heart and a humble spirit be accepted in place of the burnt offerings no longer possible (verses 25 to 45 in that numbering). A short narrative follows: the king's servants stoke the furnace with naphtha, pitch, tow, and brushwood until the flame kills the Chaldeans standing near it, and the angel of the Lord comes down and drives the fire out of the middle (verses 46 to 50). Then the three sing together (verses 51 to 90). The setting is the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 3:1). The hymn calls the three by their Hebrew birth names, Hananyah (חֲנַנְיָה), Azaryah (עֲזַרְיָה), and Mishael (מִישָׁאֵל), meaning "Yahuah has been gracious," "Yahuah has helped," and "who is what God is"; the Babylonian court had renamed them Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego (Daniel 1:7).

Both halves of the hymn became fixed canticles of the daily office. The section beginning "Blessed are you, O Lord, God of our ancestors" (verses 52 to 56) is the canticle Benedictus es, Domine. The longer section beginning "Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord" (verses 57 to 88) is the Benedicite, named from its Latin incipit Benedicite, omnia opera Domini, Domino, which renders the Greek imperative eulogeite (εὐλογεῖτε), "bless." The Roman office appoints the Benedicite at Lauds on Sundays and feasts, and the Book of Common Prayer sets it at Morning Prayer. In the Byzantine rite the two halves are the seventh and eighth of the nine biblical odes that give the canon at Orthros its pattern: the seventh ode is Azariah's prayer (verses 26 to 45) and the eighth is the Song of the Three (verses 52 to 88).

The Councils of Hippo (AD 393) and Carthage (AD 397 and 419) received Daniel with its Greek portions, as did the Council of Florence (1442) and the Council of Trent (1546), and the Orthodox churches receive it as part of Daniel. The 1611 King James Bible separates it out and prints it in the Apocrypha as the Song of the Three Children, first of the three Daniel additions, ahead of the History of Susanna and Bel and the Dragon. Because it is a stretch of Daniel 3 in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles rather than a book, a reader looking for it under this title will normally find it inside that chapter.
